ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.notes: peeled, halved or cut into 3-4cm cubes

ingredients.name: Unroasted Sri Lankan curry powder
ingredients.notes: this is a mild 'white curry' style dish; roasted curry powder makes it darker and stronger

ingredients.name: Thin coconut milk
ingredients.notes: 3/4 cup; used during the main cook

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.notes: 1/2 cup; added at the end; do not boil vigorously after adding

steps.instruction: Peel and cut the potatoes into even-sized pieces. Parboil in salted water for 10 minutes until just beginning to soften but not fully cooked -- this helps them absorb the spiced coconut milk better in the final stage. Drain and set aside.
Heat the coconut oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add the fenugreek, curry leaves, pandan leaf, cinnamon, and cardamom and sauté for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion, garlic, and green chilli. Cook until the onion is soft and lightly golden, about 3-4 minutes.
Add the turmeric, curry powder, and salt. Stir briefly to coat the aromatics.
Add the parboiled potato pieces. Pour in the thin coconut milk (or water). Bring to a gentle boil, then cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 12-15 minutes until the potatoes are fully tender.
Pour in the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer on low heat for 2-3 minutes -- do not boil hard, as this causes the coconut milk to split. Taste and adjust salt.

Serve hot with rice, string hoppers, hoppers, or bread. An optional tempering of mustard seeds, dried chilli, and curry leaves fried in a little oil and poured over the finished curry adds extra flavour and aroma.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against hungrylankan.com, loveandotherspices.com, foodvoyageur.com, cookingtheglobe.com, and berrychik.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; strong agreement on the mild coconut-milk base style and the thin-then-thick coconut milk technique
notes: Ala hodi (potato white curry) is sometimes called ala kiri hodi -- it's considered a mild, gentle dish well suited for children and anyone preferring less spice, and is one of the most common Sri Lankan curries eaten alongside string hoppers, hoppers, and pittu for breakfast. A spicier dry variant called 'ala theldala' (devilled potatoes) uses the same spice base but finishes without coconut milk, instead frying the potatoes in oil with a dry temper. Parboiling the potatoes before adding to the spiced base is not strictly necessary but strongly recommended by islandsmile.org for better spice absorption and a creamier final texture.
